en.title: The conditional
en.summary: The conditional says what would happen under a certain condition.

paragraphs: A conditional sentence has an if-clause (the condition) and a main clause (the result). English has four common types, depending on whether the condition is a general fact, a real possibility, an unreal present or an unreal past.

items: If it rains, we **will stay** home.
If I had time, I **would help**.
If I had known, I **would have come**.

blocks.html:
TypeIf-clauseMain clauseMeaning
zeropresent simplepresent simplegeneral truth: If you heat ice, it melts.
firstpresent simplewill + basereal possibility: If it rains, we'll stay.
secondpast simplewould + baseunreal or unlikely now: If I won, I'd travel.
thirdpast perfectwould have + participleunreal past: If I'd known, I'd have called.

paragraphs: The if-clause can come first or second. When it comes first, a comma follows it: If it rains, we'll stay. When it comes second, there is no comma: We'll stay if it rains.

items: Wrong: **If it will rain, we'll stay.** Right: **If it rains**
Wrong: **If I would have time, I'd help.** Right: **If I had time, I'd help.**
Wrong: **If I had known, I would know.** Right: **I would have known.**
